newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Pol Pot close to tears as denounced.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Pol Pot close to tears as denounced.

text.p: Reviled Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot was close to tears as he was denounced by his former comrades at a show trial in northern Cambodia late last week, an American journalist who witnessed the scene said.

Nate Thayer, a correspondent with the Far Eastern Economic Review, said in a press release on Monday that a white-haired and ill looking Pol Pot, dressed in simple peasant clothes, listened in silence as he was condemned by a succession of speakers and had to be helped away after he was sentenced to life in prison.
"You could see the anguish on his face as he was denounced by his former loyalists. He was close to tears," Thayer said in the release issued by his magazine.
Pol Pot was the architect of the Khmer Rouge's "killing fields" rule from 1975-79 during which more than a million Cambodians were killed by execution, torture, disease, starvation or hard labour.

Thayer, the first foreign journalist to see Pol Pot in 18 years, said the trial in front of some 500 Khmer Rouge cadres was clearly stage-managed but he said there was no doubt Pol Pot's downfall was genuine.
"This is not a hoax, this is not a ruse. Pol Pot is finished," he said. "The Khmer Rouge as we have known them no longer exist."

Khmer Rouge radio first denounced Pol Pot, now almost 70, in mid-June, shortly after a bloody split in the secretive Maoist group's top leadership in which defence chief Son Sen and almost a dozen members of his family were slaughtered.

Pol Pot and three of his commanders were found guilty of murdering Son Sen and his family, of "destroying national reconciliation" and of stealing money from the party, Thayer said. The three commanders were also said to have raped the wives of their comrades, he said.
But in Phnom Penh, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen said on Monday that Pol Pot was still in charge of the rebel group and was playing a political game.
"It is a political game of the Khmer Rouge. Pol Pot is in Anlong Veng. He is the leader of the Khmer Rouge forces," the strongman leader said.
Hun Sen, who ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh in a bloody takeover on July 6, did not elaborate on what kind of political game he thought Pol Pot was playing.
Hun Sen said the Khmer Rouge's political leader Khieu Samphan could not control the guerrilla group. "Khieu Samphan cannot control the Khmer Rouge hardliners, so Pol Pot must keep power," he said.
Bitter disagreement over how to handle the Khmer Rouge between the two premiers was a key factor leading to Hun Sen's ouster of Ranariddh.
The prince was negotiating with the rebels prior to his overthrow and was trying to secure the arrest of Pol Pot and strike a political alliance with Khieu Samphan.
Since his ouster the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group has made clear it supports the prince, repeatedly criticising Hun Sen's power-grab in its radio broadcasts.

Political analysts said the royalists and the Khmer Rouge probably still wanted to form an alliance but Pol Pot would have to be seen to be finished before the royalists could seal a deal with the remnants of the Khmer Rouge led by Khieu Samphan.
Khmer Rouge radio on Monday blasted a parliament session expected to approve the country's foreign minister Ung Huot to succeed Ranariddh as first prime minister.
It likened the session to a play being directed by Hun Sen.
Ung Huot's nomination was backed by Hun Sen while Ranariddh, who left Cambodia before he was ousted, said he has expelled the foreign minister from his royalist party.
